units.text: How do you rehost a server without waiting until cutover to transfer every disk? In the agent-based workflow shown here, the replication agent sends changed disk blocks to a staging area in A W S. That gives you replicated data to test against while the source server is still operating.

Launch a test instance and check the application, connectivity and performance. Keep production traffic on the source until the planned cutover. Confirm that replication is healthy and caught up, stop source operations for the switch, then validate the new production instance before finalizing.
The test instance is your rehearsal, not the new production service. Check that the application starts, reaches its test dependencies, and behaves correctly without moving production users to it.

Before redirecting traffic, verify settings specific to production: instance size, I A M roles, security groups, current data, and the D N S change. Know how you will back out before you start, and do not confuse a successful test launch with a verified production cutover.

At portfolio scale, start with assessed workloads rather than transforming every server the same way. For supported use cases, A W S Transform turns inventory and workload information into a proposed path. Migration orchestration and modernization are related, but they are not the same decision.

Check the proposed architecture, transformation steps, and tests before anyone approves them. A generated plan can speed up assessment; it cannot certify that the changed system still satisfies business requirements.
DataSync is the choice when you have files or objects to transfer and need a task you can schedule and verify. The transfer does not replace how the source application accesses storage day to day.

Storage Gateway addresses a different need: on-premises applications continue using familiar storage interfaces while the gateway connects to A W S storage. Choose it when preserving that hybrid workflow matters.

If an external partner already sends files over S F T P, Transfer Family provides a managed endpoint and writes to its configured storage. Start with the required protocol and client workflow, rather than assuming every transfer is a bulk-copy task.

A database migration has two separate questions: how to move rows, and whether the destination understands the source schema and code. For this same-engine example, check compatibility first; D M S can copy data and replicate changes where supported.

When switching engines, do not expect replication to translate every data type, procedure, or S Q L feature. Assess conversion, review unsupported objects, and validate the result before the data move. A W S S C T or D M S Schema Conversion can help for supported engine pairs.

Full load creates the target baseline. Change data capture then carries ongoing inserts, updates, and deletes from source logs for a supported configuration, so the target can catch up without asking the application to stop for the whole copy.

Compare source and target results, then check replication latency and errors. During the agreed cutover window, quiesce writes and verify that outstanding changes have applied before redirecting the application. A task that merely says it is running is not proof the databases match.

Start with actual network throughput. If the source continues to change while you copy, allow time for the final delta as well as the bulk transfer. Network transfer fits only if the achievable rate and change volume leave a workable cutover window.

If the bulk copy cannot fit, evaluate availability of A W S Data Transfer Terminal. Bring your devices to a supported facility and transfer over its high-speed network. Validate the completed import and still plan a final sync for changes made after the copy.

Replatform the parts that benefit from managed services without rewriting every dependency. Choose containers or functions based on the execution model, verify engine compatibility before moving a database, and distinguish object storage from a shared file system. Test application behavior, permissions, and recovery after each substitution.

The façade makes an incremental migration possible. Route one capability, such as updating a customer profile, to the new service. Requests for capabilities not yet migrated continue to the monolith, so you can verify a smaller change.

Publish an event where other systems need to react to the profile change, and decide who owns each write. If old and new systems temporarily use shared data, make the boundary explicit and plan how to remove it. Otherwise two different paths may silently disagree.

Start with business behavior, not with the number of boxes. An order service should have a clear reason to exist and a clear owner for its data. Map its synchronous calls so you can see which dependencies still control its latency and failure behavior.

Extract one capability with a measurable contract, then monitor how the app behaves when it succeeds or fails. Keep a rollback path. Decide what to extract next using those outcomes, not just the fact that the first service was deployed.

Start by inventorying interfaces, batch schedules, encodings and dependencies. The migration can fail even when the code runs if a nightly batch assumes a data format or timing the new environment no longer provides.

Rehost when preserving current behavior is the immediate priority; replatform when a supported managed component removes operational work; refactor when the application itself needs to change. The A W S services shown are possible targets, not places where any mainframe binary can run unchanged.

Modern clients enter through a façade rather than reaching into the legacy application directly. An adapter translates where the old protocol or data format differs. If an existing flow already relies on a supported broker protocol, retain that contract with an appropriate broker.

Publish asynchronous events for consumers that can process changes independently, such as reporting. Keep authentication and authorization at the boundary, and check retry, ordering, and idempotency requirements before relying on that asynchronous path.

Exercise the runbook before the actual cutover. Validate the target, stop or control writes on the source, and confirm the final data sync. Switch traffic only at the agreed gate. D N S cache expiry influences how fast clients see the change; the configured T T L does not guarantee instant movement.

Run a representative client transaction against the new environment and check operational signals. If a stop criterion fires, follow the rollback plan, including how writes made at the target will be reconciled. Hand over ownership only after the checks pass.

What breaks if you move the database before the application can reach it? Map the web, application and database tiers and their network requirements. Rehost the application tiers where that meets the objective, and choose a compatible managed database only after checking what the application expects.

Replicate the database and let test users exercise the complete path: load balancer, application, and database. Verify real transactions and monitoring before switching traffic. Keep the source available for the planned stabilization and rollback window rather than decommissioning it immediately.

For a database cutover with a short write freeze, do the bulk work early. Assess and convert the schema if the destination uses a different engine. Run full load and change data capture where supported so there is less data left to apply during the freeze.

Reconcile the target data, check replication lag, stop source writes, and confirm the last changes applied before pointing the application at the target. Keep monitoring transactions and errors afterward. Keeping the old database alone is not enough to roll back if the target has already accepted new writes.
